title: When to Fine-Tune & Data
scopeHtml: Scope: Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning, data collection and quality.

notes.title: Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning
notes.html:
What each lever changes.

Lever What changes Persistence Cost to change
Prompting instructions and examples at inference time per request seconds, free
RAG which external facts are available index content minutes, cheap
Fine-tuning the model's weights (behaviour, style, skills) permanent until retrained hours/days, data + compute + eval
Tools access to live data and actions integration engineering

Decision framework. Ask what is wrong:

  1. The model doesn't know the facts (private, new, changing) → RAG (or tools for live data). Fine-tuning is a poor and costly way to inject facts: it's unreliable at memorizing, hard to update, and gives no citations.
  2. The model knows but doesn't behave the way I need (format, tone, domain conventions, consistent style, reliable tool use) → prompting first; if prompts get long/fragile or small-model cost/latency matters → fine-tuning.
  3. Needs both → fine-tune for behaviour, RAG for knowledge.
  4. Latency/cost at scale → fine-tune a smaller model (distillation) to replace long prompts and large models.
  5. Needs actions/real-time data → tools.

Order of attack. Better prompt + examples → add retrieval → add tools → fine-tune → (rarely) continued pretraining. Each step should be justified by an eval gap.

Real life. Briefing a chef (prompt), handing them a recipe book (RAG), sending them to culinary school (fine-tuning), giving them a phone to call the supplier (tools).

Interview angle. The classic: "Should we fine-tune to teach the model our documentation?" Answer: RAG for facts; fine-tune only for behaviour.

notes.title: When fine-tuning is worth it
notes.html:
Good reasons.

  • Consistent format or voice that prompts can't hold reliably (strict JSON dialects, brand tone, clinical note style).
  • Narrow, high-volume task where a small tuned model matches a large prompted model at 10 to 100x lower cost and latency.
  • Removing long prompts/few-shot examples (they cost tokens on every call) by baking behaviour into weights.
  • Domain skills with specialized vocabulary or conventions (legal clauses, medical coding, internal DSLs, code style).
  • Improved tool-calling reliability for your specific API surface.
  • Distillation from a stronger model into a cheaper one.
  • On-device/offline or privacy-constrained deployments with open-weight models.
  • Behaviour alignment (refusal policy, safety style) with preference tuning.

Bad reasons. "Teach it our docs" (use RAG); fixing hallucinations about changing facts; compensating for no eval; avoiding prompt engineering effort; expecting to fix reasoning capability limits of a small model.

Checklist before starting.

  1. A baseline: best-effort prompting (with examples) on the target model and a stronger one.
  2. A measurable eval and a target (e.g. ≥ 95% format-valid, ≥ X accuracy, cost ≤ Y).
  3. Enough quality data (see below) or a plan to produce it.
  4. Maintenance plan: retraining when requirements change; versioning.
  5. Cost-benefit: training + hosting vs prompt tokens saved.

Real life. Train a specialist when the job is repeated thousands of times; don't send someone to school for a one-off errand.

notes.title: Data: the main determinant of quality
notes.html:
Quantity vs quality. For instruction/behaviour tuning, a few hundred to a few thousand high-quality, diverse examples often beat tens of thousands of noisy ones (the "less is more" finding). Larger sets help for complex skills or new domains.

Sourcing.

  • Production logs (best distribution match) filtered for good outcomes and cleaned/anonymized.
  • Expert demonstrations written or corrected by domain experts.
  • Synthetic data generated by a stronger model from seed tasks, then filtered with validators/judges/execution checks and diversified; always include real data in the mix.
  • Public datasets (check licences).
  • Corrections collected from user edits and human review (high value: they target real errors).

Quality criteria. Correct; consistent style and format; matches the exact prompt format and chat template used at inference; diverse in topics, lengths, difficulty; includes edge cases, refusals, "unknown", and tool-error recovery; de-duplicated; free of PII/secrets and licence-restricted content; balanced across classes/categories.

Splits and leakage. Train/validation/test split by group (not random rows) so near-duplicates or the same customer don't leak across splits; hold out a test set that is never used for tuning.

Annotation process. Clear guidelines with examples; calibration rounds; measure inter-annotator agreement; audit samples; track label noise; iterate on guidelines.

Real life. Teaching by good worked examples, not by volume of homework.

notes.title: Data formats and pitfalls
notes.html:
Formats.

  • Instruction/SFT: {"messages": [{"role":"system"},{"role":"user"},{"role":"assistant"}]}; loss on assistant tokens only; multi-turn supported; include tool calls and tool results in the same schema used at inference.
  • Completion format for base models.
  • Preference data (DPO): {prompt, chosen, rejected}.
  • Classification/regression heads or labels as text.
  • Reasoning traces (chain-of-thought) for distillation of reasoning.

Pitfalls.

  • Template mismatch between training and inference (silent quality loss).
  • Label noise and inconsistent style (the model averages them).
  • Contamination of the eval set with training data.
  • Training on model outputs where the provider's terms prohibit it.
  • PII and secrets memorized and regurgitated.
  • Overly narrow data causing catastrophic forgetting of general abilities.
  • Over-represented patterns (the model learns shortcuts, e.g. always answering "yes").
  • Truncation: training examples exceeding max length cut mid-answer.
  • Class imbalance and missing negative/edge examples.
  • Distribution shift between curated data and real traffic.

Real life. Garbage in the textbook, garbage in the student.

notes.title: Build the eval first
notes.html:
Process.

  1. Define target behaviours and metrics (accuracy/F1, format validity, rubric score, latency, cost, safety).
  2. Build a held-out test set that reflects production, including hard and adversarial cases and general-capability probes (to detect forgetting).
  3. Baseline: evaluate the base model with the best prompt; evaluate a stronger model as an upper reference.
  4. Fine-tune; evaluate on the same set with the same grader; compare with confidence intervals.
  5. Check regressions: general benchmarks, safety/refusal behaviour, other tasks.
  6. Evaluate cost/latency/serving requirements.
  7. Decide: ship, iterate on data/hyperparameters, or abandon if the gain doesn't justify the cost.

If you cannot measure improvement, do not fine-tune.

Real life. Take a "before" photo so you can tell whether the diet worked.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Choosing the lever. Prompting for quick behaviour/format control; RAG for knowledge (private, fresh, large, with citations); tools for live data/actions; fine-tuning for stable behaviour, style, narrow high-volume tasks, lower cost/latency, shorter prompts, distillation. Fine-tuning is a poor way to add facts.

Worth it when. Prompts can't hold format/voice; a small tuned model can replace a large prompted one; long few-shot prompts are costly; domain conventions or tool reliability need to improve. Prerequisites: baseline, eval, data, maintenance plan.

Data. Quality and diversity beat volume; use real logs, expert demonstrations, filtered synthetic data and corrections; match the inference template exactly; include edge cases and refusals; de-duplicate; split by group; watch PII and licences.

Pitfalls. Template mismatch, label noise, contamination, forgetting, shortcuts, truncation, distribution shift, terms-of-use violations.

Evaluate first. Held-out test set, baselines (prompted base and stronger model), regression checks, cost/latency; no measurable gain means no fine-tune.

Interview one-liners.

  • "RAG is for knowledge, fine-tuning is for behaviour."
  • "Data quality is the model."
  • "Train on exactly the format you will serve."
  • "No eval, no fine-tune."
